details.definition: Computation as the evaluation of functions over values, avoiding mutable state and side effects.
details.does: Treats functions as ordinary values, prefers transformation of immutable data over in-place mutation, and confines effects to declared places.
details.outcome: Local reasoning — a function's behaviour depends only on its arguments, so it can be tested, cached, reordered and parallelised. Paid for in allocation and unfamiliar idiom.
details.motivation: Shared mutable state makes it impossible to know what a function does without knowing everything that can reach its inputs. Removing mutation removes that dependence.
details.origin: Church's lambda calculus (1930s) gave the model; McCarthy's LISP (1958) made it executable; Backus's 1977 Turing lecture 'Can Programming Be Liberated from the von Neumann Style?' made it a design argument against the assignment statement.
details.first_principles: Referential transparency means an expression can be replaced by its value without changing meaning. That single property is what licenses memoisation, common-subexpression elimination, reordering and safe parallelism.

details.definition: Programs organised as objects that bundle state with the operations permitted on it, selected at call time by the object's own type.

details.definition: You state the result you want; an engine chooses the procedure that produces it.
details.does: Separates specification from execution strategy, handing traversal, ordering and optimisation to a planner, solver or runtime.

details.definition: Independent actors each own private state and communicate only by asynchronous messages delivered to a mailbox addressed by identity.
details.does: Removes shared memory entirely: an actor processes one message at a time, may change its own state, send messages, and create new actors.
details.outcome: Failure is contained — an actor can crash without corrupting anyone else, so supervision and restart become viable. Bought with message-copying cost and no shared-memory speed.
details.motivation: Ericsson needed telephone switches that stay up while parts fail, across machines. Shared memory cannot span machines, and locks cannot contain a crash mid-mutation.
details.origin: Hewitt, Bishop and Steiger, 1973, as a model of concurrent computation. Armstrong's Erlang (Ericsson, late 1980s) made it industrial, with 'let it crash' and supervision trees as the operational doctrine.
details.first_principles: If two components share no memory, one cannot corrupt the other's state by failing. Isolation is what makes partial failure recoverable — and it is also exactly what a network boundary already imposes, which is why the model survives distribution unchanged.

empowered_by.forCase: Making GC pauses per-actor rather than global — a concrete reason Erlang achieves soft-real-time behaviour that a shared-heap runtime cannot.

empowered_by.forCase: Guaranteeing fairness — one runaway process cannot starve the scheduler, unlike cooperative event loops.

details.definition: Whether the type of an expression is fixed and checked before the program runs, or carried by values and checked as it runs.
details.does: Static checking rejects ill-typed programs at compile time; dynamic checking attaches a tag to every value and verifies operations at each use.
details.outcome: Static catches a class of errors before deployment and enables optimisation; dynamic removes annotation burden and permits programs a checker would reject. The trade is when you find out.
details.motivation: Untyped machine code lets you add a string to a pointer. Every type system since negotiates how much it rejects against how much it costs to satisfy.
details.origin: Type theory from Russell (1900s) via Church's typed lambda calculus (1940); ALGOL 60 brought declared types to mainstream languages; Milner's 1978 polymorphic inference made static typing cheap to write.
details.first_principles: A type is a static over-approximation of the values an expression can take. Rice's theorem means any sound checker must reject some correct programs — soundness and completeness cannot both hold, so every type system chooses which errors to tolerate.

details.definition: An algorithm that deduces the most general type of an expression with no annotations, and does so completely for its fragment of the type system.

details.definition: You call malloc to reserve bytes and free to release them. The compiler tracks nothing; correctness is entirely a property of your discipline.
details.does: Reserves a byte range on the heap and hands back its address. Nothing records who owns it, how long it lives, or whether anyone still points at it.
details.outcome: Total control over layout and timing, and personal liability for four bug classes: use-after-free, double-free, buffer overflow, and leaks.
details.motivation: Programs need memory whose size or lifetime isn't known at compile time. The stack can't do it — it dies at scope exit. Something had to hand out long-lived storage.
details.origin: C, early 1970s (Ritchie, Bell Labs). malloc/free formalised in ANSI C (1989). Predates every automatic scheme here — all of them are answers to its failure modes.
details.first_principles: RAM is a flat addressable array. 'Allocation' is pure bookkeeping — a free-list the allocator keeps in ordinary memory. Nothing in the hardware knows an object exists or has died.

empowered_by.how: The allocator requests large page-aligned regions from the kernel and then sub-allocates within them; glibc malloc uses brk for the main arena and mmap for allocations above MMAP_THRESHOLD (128 KB by default).
empowered_by.forCase: Obtaining backing pages at all — malloc cannot create memory, only parcel out what the kernel maps.

empowered_by.how: glibc keeps size-segregated bins (fast, small, large, unsorted) of previously freed chunks; each chunk carries an 8/16-byte header holding its size and flags.
empowered_by.forCase: Making free() O(1) in the common case and letting a later malloc reuse the block without a syscall.

empowered_by.how: The returned pointer is a virtual address; the MMU walks page tables to reach physical DRAM, and pages may not be resident until first touch.
empowered_by.forCase: Giving every process a private flat address space, which is why two processes can both hold address 0x600000 without colliding.

empowered_by.how: free(p) locates the chunk header by subtracting a fixed offset from p — a plain integer subtraction on the address.
empowered_by.forCase: Recovering allocation metadata from a bare pointer, since free() is given no size argument.

details.definition: The runtime periodically determines which objects are still reachable from live roots and reclaims everything else. You never call free.
details.does: Traces references from a root set (stack, globals, registers) through the object graph, marks what it finds, and reclaims the rest.
details.outcome: Whole bug classes disappear — no use-after-free, no double-free. In exchange you surrender control of *when* memory is released, and accept pause times.
details.motivation: Manual free is provably error-prone at scale. If reachability can be computed, the machine can decide the free point better than a human tracking it across a large codebase.
details.origin: McCarthy, LISP, 1959 — invented because list structure made manual freeing intractable. The oldest automatic-memory idea in computing.

empowered_by.forCase: Deciding liveness — reachability is the operational definition of 'not garbage', so the traversal *is* the liveness test.

details.definition: The concrete algorithm behind most collectors: mark everything reachable from the roots, then sweep (or compact) whatever wasn't marked.
details.does: Two phases. Mark walks the reference graph setting a bit per live object. Sweep walks the heap linearly, reclaiming unmarked cells.
details.outcome: Collects cycles that reference counting cannot, at the cost of touching a large fraction of the heap and needing a pause — or heavy machinery to avoid one.

details.definition: A single thread runs a loop: take the next ready callback, run it to completion, repeat. All I/O is non-blocking and completes by queueing a callback.
details.does: Polls the OS readiness interface, drains the microtask queue after every task, and executes callbacks one at a time with no preemption.
details.outcome: No locks, no data races, no shared-memory bugs — because only one thread ever touches your data. And no CPU parallelism: one long computation freezes everything.
details.motivation: A browser must stay responsive while waiting on the network, with a single-threaded DOM. Threads plus a mutable DOM would have been a disaster, so the concurrency went into I/O rather than execution.
details.origin: The reactor pattern predates it, but the browser's JS engine made it the default for a generation; Node.js (Dahl, 2009) carried it to the server via libuv.
details.first_principles: Concurrency and parallelism are different. Interleaving *waiting* needs one thread; only interleaving *computing* needs several. The event loop exploits the fact that most server work is waiting.

empowered_by.how: Each turn runs fixed phases — timers, pending callbacks, poll, check (setImmediate), close — in a defined order.
empowered_by.forCase: Giving deterministic callback ordering; it is the concrete reason setTimeout(...,0) and setImmediate can fire in different orders.

empowered_by.how: After each macrotask the engine empties the microtask queue completely, including all resolved Promise continuations.
empowered_by.forCase: Promise semantics specifically — this is why an await resumes before the next timer, and why an infinite microtask chain starves the loop.

empowered_by.how: One syscall reports readiness for thousands of descriptors at once.
